question:
Patient note:
A 31-year-old woman is evaluated in the ambulatory orthopaedic bay this morning for a right knee diagnostic and therapeutic arthroscopy to address persistent mechanical clicking and episodic locking following an anterior cruciate ligament sprain sustained while trail-running eight months ago; the attending anticipates roughly thirty minutes of insufflation and portal work under general anaesthesia with discharge later today if she tolerates weight bearing. She strode from the parking structure carrying her own backpack, negotiated two flights of stairs easily, and has been working full time as a graphic designer, cycling to the office most days, which confirms her usual level of activity is unrestricted. The present encounter is her first trip to an operating room in more than a year, she has not had any operations in the past thirty days, and she has not undergone any endoscopic, interventional radiology, or open procedures during the past several weeks. Three weeks ago, however, she completed a five-day inpatient stay on the medicine ward for multilobar community-acquired pneumonia that presented with fever to 39 °C, productive cough, and transient oxygen saturation of 91 % on ambient air; throughout the admission she remained haemodynamically stable, blood cultures were sterile, and no sepsis criteria were met. A peripherally inserted central catheter was placed in the left basilic vein on hospital day two to facilitate high-dose intravenous ceftriaxone and has remained in situ because outpatient antimicrobial therapy continued for ten additional days. The line is visible today beneath a transparent film, flushes without resistance, aspirates briskly with dark venous blood, and there is no surrounding erythema, drainage, or tenderness along the track. She reports that the respiratory infection has resolved, she has been afebrile for ten days, and her energy has returned to baseline. Past medical history is notable for ileocolonic Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 19, currently in clinical remission on adalimumab 40 mg every other week; her last colonoscopy six months ago showed only minimal aphthous ulceration and no dysplasia. During an insurance evaluation two years ago, fasting homocysteine was found to be mildly elevated at 17 µmol L-¹; she was advised to supplement folate and vitamin B12, which she takes most mornings. She denies congestive heart-failure symptoms, has never been treated for bacteremia apart from the recent pneumonia, and has no history of chronic lung disease beyond occasional asthma-like wheeze in childhood that resolved by adolescence. She has never worn a plaster cast, never fractured her hip, pelvis, or long bones, and has had no spinal cord injuries or strokes. There is no personal record of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolus, and she recounts no episodes of unilateral leg swelling, cord-like tenderness, or unexplained chest pain; first-degree relatives similarly have no venous clotting events. Genetic testing for common thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden or the prothrombin G20210A mutation was performed last summer and returned negative, and an autoimmune work-up last year showed negative antiphospholipid antibodies. She has never been exposed to unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin outside of routine catheter flushes and has not experienced thrombocytopenia. She does not smoke, takes a single glass of wine on weekends, and denies recreational drugs; body-mass index at check-in is 23 kg m-². Medications this morning include adalimumab (last dose nine days ago), oral folic acid 1 mg, cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg, and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg for knee discomfort; she has never used systemic corticosteroids for more than a tapering burst and is not on hormonal contraception, selective oestrogen-receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs. Review of systems is negative for dyspnoea, orthopnoea, chest tightness, palpitations, abdominal pain, bloody stool, or recent unintentional weight change. Vital signs obtained fifteen minutes ago record temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 114/68 mm Hg, heart rate 74 beats min-¹ in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 min-¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing room air. Examination shows an alert, conversational woman reclining comfortably. Sclerae are anicteric, oral mucosa moist, neck supple without jugular distention. Cardiac auscultation reveals crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; peripheral pulses are 2 +/4 and equal bilaterally. Lungs are clear to auscultation with full excursion and no wheeze. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with normoactive bowel sounds; there is a well-healed 3 cm periumbilical diagnostic laparoscopic scar from a remote appendectomy but no masses or organomegaly. Inspection of both lower extremities shows the right knee slightly swollen compared with the left but without erythema; patellar glide elicits a palpable click, and anterior drawer is 1+ lax. Calves are supple, non-tender, and measure 35 cm circumference bilaterally, with no varicosities or pitting oedema. The PICC dressing on the left upper arm is clean, dry, and occlusive. Neurologic screening yields full orientation, intact cranial nerves, and 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups except mild discomfort-limited quadriceps activation on the operative side. A single 20-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter is in the right forearm running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no additional vascular devices are present. Pre-operative laboratories drawn through the PICC at 06:00 reveal haemoglobin 13.4 g dL-¹, haematocrit 40 %, platelet count 252 × 10⁹ L-¹, leukocytes 6.2 × 10⁹ L-¹, sodium 139 mmol L-¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L-¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L-¹, creatinine 0.78 mg dL-¹, AST 18 U L-¹, ALT 20 U L-¹, total bilirubin 0.6 mg dL-¹, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats min-¹ with preserved intervals and no ST-T abnormality. A posterior-anterior chest radiograph obtained two days ago to confirm catheter tip position demonstrates clear lungs, a normal mediastinal silhouette, and the catheter terminus at the cavo-atrial junction. Sequential compression sleeves are wrapped around both calves but have not yet been activated, and chemoprophylaxis has been withheld until after skin closure given the short duration of the case. She has been nil per os since midnight, voided at 0700 without dysuria, removed earrings and piercings, and verbalises understanding of the operative plan along with the expectation of crutch-assisted ambulation on discharge later today.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums weighted preoperative risk factors.
- Pneumonia within the preceding month: hospitalized for multilobar pneumonia three weeks ago → 1. Resolution does not remove this recent risk factor.
- History of inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn’s disease, even in remission → 1.
- Arthroscopic surgery: planned knee arthroscopy → 2. Do not also count the same procedure as minor surgery.
- Central venous access: the indwelling PICC terminates at the cavo-atrial junction → 2. The peripheral IV adds nothing.
- Elevated homocysteine: previously measured at 17 µmol/L → 3.
- Other factors: age 31, BMI 23, unrestricted mobility, no qualifying leg edema, no personal or family VTE, and no estrogen use → 0. Hospitalization alone does not establish prolonged bed rest.
Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
